title: Geologic Time and Dating
seo_title: Geology 12: Geologic Time and Dating Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
short_title: relative dating, radiometric dating and the time scale
standard_text: Geologic time: relative dating principles (superposition, cross-cutting relationships, unconformities), fossils and index fossils, radiometric dating and half-life, and the geologic time scale. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Geology 12)
meta_desc: Free Geology 12 worksheets (BC Curriculum): relative dating, radiometric dating and the time scale. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Relative dating gives order; radiometric dating gives age.
key_sub: After each half-life, half the parent isotope remains.
body_html:
How to think about it

Relative dating uses principles: superposition (lower layers are older), original horizontality, cross-cutting relationships (a fault or dike is younger than the rock it cuts) and unconformities (gaps in the record). Index fossils match layers in different places.

Radiometric dating measures the ratio of parent and daughter isotopes: after one half-life 50% of the parent remains, after two 25%. The geologic time scale divides Earth's 4.6-billion-year history into eons, eras, periods and epochs.

Example

A dike cuts through three layers. Is it older or younger than the layers?

Cross-cutting

Answer: younger

Example

A rock has 25% of its parent isotope left. How many half-lives have passed?

100 → 50 → 25

Answer: 2

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a half-life is half the age of the rock.
  • Thinking the top layer is always youngest even when folded.
  • Using carbon-14 to date very old rocks.

items.q: A rock started with 64 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 5 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 64 − 2 = 62 g.

items.q: A sample starts with 100 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 3 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 3 times: 12.5 g.

items.q: A piece of old wood has 1/64 of its original carbon-14 left (half-life 5730 years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/64 = 6 half-lives; 6 × 5730 = 34380 years.

items.q: A sample had 64 g of parent and now has 4 g. How many half-lives have passed?
items.e: 64 → 4 takes 4 halvings.
